narrative:
The model estimates you have a 44% chance of leaving your job. This is high enough that the company has decided to deny your promotion, as they are focusing resources on employees more likely to stay long-term.

The prediction is driven primarily by your overall work history and current role. Your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence, pushing the model toward expecting you to stay. Having only 1-5 years of total experience is common among those predicted to remain (half of that group falls in this range), yet in your case the model interpreted this limited experience as a stabilizing factor rather than a risk.

Two other factors worked against you and ultimately tipped the balance toward leaving. The length of time you have spent in your current organization (also 1-5 years) was the second most important signal and pulled the prediction toward departure. Similarly, not having received any other job offers while working here ranked third and also nudged the model to expect you might leave.

Taken together, the combination of short tenure in your present role and the absence of external opportunities signaled higher turnover risk, outweighing the stabilizing effect of your modest overall experience.

The organization should consider discussing your career goals openly with you and exploring whether additional support, clearer promotion paths, or targeted development could increase your commitment. You may want to reflect on what would make staying feel more rewarding.
